notes:
Two findings that were true, and worded in a way that made them wrong.

Both of these came out of auditing a municipal transit authority and then checking every medium and high against the live site — not from a bug report. Nothing was failing; the findings fired on real defects. What was wrong was the sentence each one printed.

**A redirect that leaves your site was drawn as coming back to it.** When a URL redirects somewhere off your domain, Docket deliberately keeps your URL on the record rather than adopting the destination — the content at the far end is not yours, and attributing it to you would be a worse bug. But the sentence that writes out the chain always ended it with your URL, so an off-site redirect printed as `/survey → thirdparty.example/login → /survey`. That describes a redirect **loop**, which is a different and more serious defect with its own critical check. Two of the three chains on the site we audited read that way. One of them leaves the agency's domain for a site they do not own and returns a 404 — genuinely worth knowing, and not what the report said. Chains that stay on your site were always correct, which is why this survived: it was invisible on exactly the examples the code was written against.

**A spam trap was counted as a field you should delete.** Docket already knew not to count honeypots — the hidden field a form adds to catch bots, which a real visitor never sees — and its own code says why: those fields cannot be cut, because they are the trap. It checked whether the field itself was marked invisible. Every common framework puts that marking on the wrapper around the field instead. So on a "Report a Biohazard" form, Docket counted eleven fields and advised cutting some, when the eleventh was the spam trap. It now reads the wrapper too, and the count on that form is ten.

That fix is deliberately narrow. A multi-step form hides its later steps the same way, and those fields are real — the form genuinely is that long, and quietly dropping them would understate it. A honeypot sits alone in its hidden wrapper; a step does not.

**Also:** an internal check that guards against Docket's own build silently changing shape could pass while reading nothing at all. It asserted that certain strings are absent from the shipped binary, without ever confirming it had read the binary successfully — so a failed read looked exactly like a clean result. It now checks for a string it knows is there before trusting the absences. Raised by a sibling project that lost hours to the same shape.
